design_judgment.intended_result: The set now states one coherent product result and one reader decision per layer. The Charter answers whether a capability belongs to Runtime, the T0 answers which identity survives provider and backend replacement, the T1 answers which single owner holds a responsibility and in which direction it may depend, and each T2 answers one implementable question. The public host lifecycle enumerates identically across Charter section 7 item 3, T0 section 6, T1 section 5.1, and Execution section 2 (start, bounded status and result refs, cancel, authorized external event, reconcile, recover), so the Charter completion gate cannot pass while a required public operation is absent. The material choices are stated and defended rather than assumed: six peer responsibilities plus four supporting or validating T2s, one canonical Ledger, per-responsibility Policy Enforcement Points instead of a central authorization service, idempotent reconciliation instead of a claimed cross-system transaction, and an offline Inspection export that is a governed derivative response rather than a third store. Revision 1's twelve carried findings are genuinely closed against the revised text, not merely asserted closed: I verified the T0 section 3.2 Runtime Execution registration (f01), the T1 section 6 per-origin start ordering (f02), the conditional Workflow Execution binding in Invocation section 2 and conformance item 13 (f03), the Source Architecture rule 6 host-validator resolution and conformance item 12 (f04), the Registry section 3 Execution Variant Policy family with section 10 rejection rows and conformance item 21 (f05), the non-persistent export in T1 section 9.3 and Inspection sections 6 and 9 item 10 (f06), the removal of the partial frontmatter inherits key in Ingress (f07), the host-neutral wording in Conformance sections 3, 4, and 9 (f08), the corrected 21-item enumeration evidence in the t2_candidate manifest (f09), the two added foundation edges in T1 section 3 (f10), the removed PostgreSQL preference in Invocation section 4 (f11), and the both-origin lineage view and reader gain in Inspection sections 4 and the header (f12).
design_judgment.authority_structure: Each of the six responsibilities has exactly one primary T2 owner in T1 section 2, and documents 02, 03, 05, and 09 are explicitly scoped as specializing or validating rather than peer. No seventh responsibility is smuggled in: the supporting foundation, physical directories, repository planes, PostgreSQL, Temporal, and providers are each labelled as a source class, plane, or replaceable binding. Duplicated authority is actively refused at every point where it could appear: Registry section 8 makes the Registry writer its own enforcement point and disclaims dependence on document 09's ports; document 09 section 4 disclaims becoming a central PEP; Ledger section 6 owns durable fence comparison while 09 owns fence meaning and 10 owns finalization timing; Inspection section 1 explicitly reconciles its `get_execution` view against Execution's `get_status` so neither becomes a second status authority; Registry validates Variant Policy schema and Profile admission while Execution alone validates node coverage. Two authority-source gaps remain, both local. Execution section 2.1 declares itself the enforcement point for its own lifecycle actions and simultaneously excludes document 09's execution-time observation port, but unlike Registry, Invocation, and Inspection it names no decision source at all. And `InvocationHost`, a declared Invocation output granting Ledger content staging and dynamic operation authorization, has no declared provider anywhere in the set.
design_judgment.boundary_coherence: Semantic owner, author, operator, reviewer, persistence owner, implementation binding, and approval authority stay distinct almost everywhere they meet. Registry and Ledger own record and schema meaning while Data Governance binds the System of Record and writer boundary and Software Delivery admits migration code; Contract Audit owns the independent verdict while Design Doc Management owns admission of canonical text; document 05 assembles evidence and explicitly refuses to publish or deploy; the repository-plane table in Source Architecture section 7 keeps logical ownership, physical placement, packaging, and generation authority labelled rather than presented as peers. Revision 1's forbidden reverse edge is resolved cleanly: Invocation now consumes a host-provided Product Authorization decision validator through its own public boundary on the Registry pattern, and Source Architecture conformance item 12 makes that machine-checkable. The residual boundary defect is that Execution, the most privileged public surface in the set, is the only protected-resource owner whose decision source is unnamed while the one authority port it legally holds is explicitly excluded for that purpose. One term-level defect remains: T1 section 2 uses a bare 'Registry' for the Design Doc contract registry inside the same section that defines the Runtime Registry responsibility.
design_judgment.inheritance_and_dependencies: Inherited constraints are named per document and close. The Timestamp Semantics registered predicate, immutable `DistributedClockProfile`, fresh per-domain `ClockHealthEvidence`, and section 8 conservative half-open window are consumed identically by Registry section 8, Ledger sections 3 and 6, document 09 sections 3 and 6, Inspection section 2, Ingress section 7, and Execution section 6, and every one fails closed; the Ledger store alone assigns `recorded_at_utc` and Execution and Invocation both disclaim assigning it. Product Authorization's grant-class law, `ResourcePermissionManifest` obligation, and Principal-versus-workload-actor separation are consumed without redefinition, as is Data Governance's derivative-inheritance and export law, which Inspection section 6 now applies to the export rather than inventing a Runtime record family. Dependency direction is acyclic and enforceable: Source Architecture section 3 places T2 03 and T2 09 source inside Execution, so the only cross-responsibility edges are Execution to Registry, Invocation, Durability, and Ledger; Invocation to Registry; Inspection to Registry and Ledger; and everything to the foundation. The inbound `DurableDispatchSink` is correctly a Durability-owned port implemented above it, not a reverse import. One inheritance closure gap remains: T1 section 6 step 4 and Execution section 3 both require the independent Module origin's root Module Run to be part of the atomic start commit and the start-replay invariant, while Ledger section 5.1, which owns the atomic transaction families, does not list it.
design_judgment.intent_code_separation: Stable intent is well separated from mutable truth. Every T2 ends with a change boundary that refuses to freeze fields, select a provider, or migrate data; the code architecture audit's current-code observations are consistently held as evidence inputs rather than design; PostgreSQL, Temporal, Claude, and Codex appear only as excluded types or replaceable adapters; document 05 now states the general no-host-coupling rule and pushes exact excluded package identities into the code-owned conformance profile; Inspection section 13 records the concrete store binding only in the code-owned evidence record. Two residues remain. Durability section 9 keeps a numbered 'Temporal Mapping' section whose Signal, Update, query, retry, and Continue-As-New constraints are one current backend's mechanics inside stable intent, which is the same class the revision-1 f11 correction removed from Invocation. Separately, the frozen subject rewrites the portable governance law in `the_agent_runtime.md`, whose own section 12 requires the portable source to change first under the governance distribution owner, yet the manifest targets only the installed projection `designDoc/the_agent_runtime.md` and declares no portable-source or distribution-owner obligation among its adoption blockers.
design_judgment.implementability: Most of the set is implementable without redesign. Start, dispatch, protected-operation intent, finalization, event application, cancellation, invalidation, acknowledgement, recovery, and reconciliation converge idempotently across every declared crash and race window without claiming cross-system atomicity or a second Ledger. Provider and model A/B Variants, Runtime retry, durable delivery retry, reviewer revision loops, provider-context reconstruction, and new execution are each distinguished and consistently represented across documents 01, 08, and 10. Both origins are now complete: Ingress section 4 refuses a non-Workflow origin, Execution section 4 states that an independent Module origin cannot enter a wait, and Invocation conformance item 13 exercises the module origin. Inspection filters authorized scope at storage before disclosure and keeps content permissions separate. Standalone Release Conformance freezes one exact subject including generated Design Contract bundle parity and stays out of Software Delivery and Contract Audit. The set is close to minimal; `RuntimeCohesionSignalReport` remains the only object I would question on economy and it is defensible as explicitly advisory. Three implementability gaps would still force a Code Design Basis to invent semantics: the unnamed provider of `InvocationHost` together with the unassigned owner of the mid-Invocation protected-operation intent commit for dynamic tool and Gateway calls; the release-family taxonomy conflict for the Execution Variant Policy, which keys immutable identity and the activation scope; and the start-batch disagreement about the module-origin root Module Run. Each is correctable inside an existing owner without adding a layer, port, or process.

findings.quoted_evidence: Execution 10 section 2.1: "`start`, `get_status`, `reconcile`, and `recover` require a current exact authorization decision under their registered scope. External `request_cancellation` and `submit_external_event` mutate canonical execution state across a service boundary and require the bounded `OperationGrant` class unless a successor manifest deliberately admits a narrower class. Execution enforces this manifest itself and does not route its lifecycle authorization through document 09's execution-time observation port." Every peer enforcement point names its source: Registry 01 section 8 "resolves the exact lifecycle action and release resource server-side and calls a host-provided Product Authorization decision validator"; Invocation 08 section 5 "a current decision from the host-provided Product Authorization validator. Invocation does not import document 09 or Execution private source to obtain that decision."; Inspection 06 section 2 "The trusted host resolves one opaque `InspectionQueryScope` from Product Authorization before query execution." Execution 10 names none.
findings.requirement: T1 section 2 requires that "Each Runtime responsibility that owns a protected resource acts as the Policy Enforcement Point for its own operations under Product Authorization and publishes its own `ResourcePermissionManifest`", and section 12 lists "each protected-resource responsibility's own `ResourcePermissionManifest` and enforcement point" as a required machine contract. Product Authorization section 5 requires the enforcement point to "obtain or validate the current Product Authorization decision" before executing.
findings.impact: Execution is the only one of the four declared Policy Enforcement Points with no declared decision source, and the one external-authority port it legally holds under the T1 section 3 graph is explicitly excluded for this purpose. A Code Design Basis must invent one of three incompatible answers: reuse document 09's `authorize_protected_operation`, contradicting section 2.1; add an unregistered validator protocol to the Execution public surface, which Source Architecture section 6 and conformance item 4 would then not cover; or treat the host binding as already authorized and skip validation, which silently deletes the enforcement obligation on the Runtime's most privileged public surface, including `request_cancellation` and `submit_external_event` where the contract itself demands a bounded `OperationGrant`.

findings.quoted_evidence: Invocation 08 section 6: "An `InvocationHost` provides only request-bound capabilities: read one authorized semantic input handle; stage one output body under the Attempt; request current authorization for one declared dynamic operation; and invoke the admitted resource only after that authorization succeeds. For each dynamic tool call, Runtime constructs an exact operation intent before the resource callable is entered." Ledger 04 section 5.3: "Before a model call, Gateway call, external effect, or other protected operation begins, Ledger commits the exact operation identity, parent Attempt, authority-observation refs, resource/action scope, and idempotency identity. Observation after the operation cannot manufacture this prior authority." Execution 10 section 4 orders the dispatch as "4. commits every required protected-operation intent; 5. calls Invocation once for that Attempt;" and never mentions `InvocationHost`. Invocation 08 non_goals exclude "canonical Ledger writes", and the Source Architecture section 3 graph contains no INVOCATION to LEDGER edge.
findings.requirement: the_agent_runtime section 6 invariant 2 requires that "the durable intent and active fence are committed before the corresponding external effect". T1 section 7 step 4 requires that "Required protected-operation intents are committed before external access". Source Architecture section 3 rule 1 permits a responsibility to import "only the foundation, its declared inward public dependencies, and its own private implementation".
findings.impact: `InvocationHost` is a declared Invocation output that grants Ledger content staging, per-call authorization, and admitted-resource invocation, yet no document in the set names its provider. For a dynamic tool or Gateway call discovered inside an open Attempt, no owner is assigned for the required prior Ledger operation-intent commit: Invocation may not write or import Ledger, and Execution's ordered dispatch commits intents only before the single Invocation call. An implementer must invent whether Execution re-enters Ledger while an Attempt claim is open and how that commit orders against the active claim and current fence, whether Invocation acquires a forbidden Ledger edge, or whether dynamic calls proceed under a pre-authorized composite capability window. The third choice defeats the explicit rule that observation after the operation cannot manufacture prior authority, so the gap is on the security-bearing path rather than a presentational one.

findings.quoted_evidence: T1 section 6 step 4: "Ledger atomically commits the binding, active fence, start intent, and common Runtime Execution fact; for Workflow origin it also commits the Workflow Execution fact, while for independent Module origin it commits the root Module Run binding and no Workflow identity." Execution 10 section 3: "If the Ledger start exists but acknowledgement does not, `start` or `reconcile` resubmits the same durable command and commits the returned existing backend result. It creates no second Runtime Execution, Workflow Execution, or root Module Run." Ledger 04 section 5.1 enumerates the start batch without it: "One start batch commits the exact host binding, admitted Runtime release closure, external authorization context, governed-input scope, active authority fence, durable-start intent, and top-level Runtime Execution fact. A Workflow-origin start additionally commits its exact Workflow Execution fact; an independent Module origin commits `origin_kind=module`, the exact Module Release and Variant Policy refs, and no invented Workflow identity."
findings.requirement: T1 section 7 states "Document 04 owns the record and transaction families", and T1 section 0 scope includes "cross-responsibility call, commit, recovery, and acknowledgement ordering". Design Doc Management section 6 requires audit of "peer-boundary and inherited-constraint closure" and forbids a candidate whose parent and child give different rules for the same object.
findings.impact: The root's normative start ordering and Execution's start-replay invariant both treat the independent Module origin's root Module Run as part of the atomic start commit, while the owner of the atomic transaction families lists only the Module Release and Variant Policy refs. A Code Design Basis building the start batch must guess whether the root Module Run fact commits with the Runtime Execution fact or at first dispatch. That choice changes the start batch schema, the idempotent replay identity that Ledger section 3 rule 1 keys on, and what a crash between start and first dispatch leaves recoverable, so guessing wrong propagates into the recovery invariant for one of the two declared origins. This is the residue of the revision-1 f02 correction, which was applied to the root but not to the transaction-family owner.

findings.quoted_evidence: Registry 01 section 3 states "Registry admits the following logical families." and then lists both "Behavior Policy | Immutable Context, Evaluation, retry, entry, operation, or output-resolution rule referenced by a Module or Workflow" and, as a separate row, "Execution Variant Policy | A named Behavior Policy form selected by the exact host execution binding; owns ordered sibling Variant IDs, exact admitted Execution Profile refs, and their origin or Workflow-node coverage declaration". Execution 10 section 3 asserts a single classification: "The Variant Policy is an admitted Registry Behavior Policy carried as an opaque exact ref by the host binding."
findings.requirement: Registry section 2 states "Every release identity contains one release family, stable object ID, explicit version, canonical payload schema version, and SHA-256 of the canonical payload. For one `(family, object_id, version)`, exactly one canonical payload is legal." Registry section 7 states "A `RegistryActivationScope` is exactly one `(release_family, stable_object_id)` logical object."
findings.impact: The release family value keys immutable release identity and the activation scope, so an implementer cannot defer this. Registry simultaneously presents Execution Variant Policy as a peer family row and as "a named Behavior Policy form", while Execution flatly calls it a Behavior Policy; and the Behavior Policy row's own definition, "referenced by a Module or Workflow", is false for a Variant Policy that is referenced only by the host execution binding. A Code Design Basis must invent whether `execution_variant_policy` is a distinct family enum value or a discriminator inside `behavior_policy`, and whether a Variant Policy and a Behavior Policy sharing a stable object ID collide in one `RegistryActivationScope`. Registry's section 10 rejection row and section 11 item 21 both address it as a separate object, so Execution section 3 is the outlier, but the family taxonomy is Registry's to state.
